title: Lab 304 - Git and GitLab - Diff, Fetch, Merge and Pull

lab_objective.description: By the end of this lab, you should be able to:
objectives: Create a GitLab project initialized with a README and clone it to a Linux VM.
Explain the difference between the working directory, staging area, local repository, and remote repository.
Use git status and git diff to inspect unstaged changes.
Use git add and git diff --cached to inspect staged changes.
Commit and push local changes to GitLab.
Use git fetch to download remote updates without integrating them into the current branch.
Inspect remote-tracking branches such as origin/main.
Use git merge to integrate fetched changes into the current branch.
Use git pull to fetch and integrate remote changes.
Verify file contents, commit history, and repository status after synchronization.
scenario: You are a Linux Systems Administrator collaborating on project documentation stored in GitLab.
You will create a new private GitLab project and initialize it with a README file.
You will clone the project to your Linux VM and practice reviewing local changes before staging and committing them.
You will then make separate changes through the GitLab web interface to simulate a teammate updating the remote repository.
You will use git fetch and git merge as separate operations, then use git pull to retrieve and integrate another remote change.
Default branch used in this lab: main
Use the exact SSH clone URL displayed by your GitLab instance. Your namespace may be a username or a group.

tasks.title: Verify Git and Your Identity
steps: Check your configured Git name and email:
If either value is missing, configure your intended name and email address using git config --global.
concept: Git records the configured author identity in commits. GitLab hosts the remote repository; Git is the version control tool used locally.

tasks.title: Create a New GitLab Project
steps: Open https://gitlab.corp.linoop.us and sign in with your assigned account.
Create a blank project named lab304-git-workflow.
Set the project visibility to Private.
Enable the option to initialize the repository with a README.
Open the project and copy its SSH clone URL from the Code menu.
Use the exact URL displayed by your GitLab instance.
concept: Initializing the project with a README creates an initial commit and a default branch, giving you a tracked file to modify immediately after cloning.

tasks.title: Clone the Repository to Your Linux VM
steps: Create the git-labs directory in your home directory if it does not already exist:
Clone the project using the SSH URL copied from GitLab:
Verify your current directory and list the files.
Use the actual SSH URL from GitLab, replacing the example namespace.
concept: git clone creates a local copy of the repository and its history and normally configures the remote repository under the name origin.

tasks.title: Inspect the Initial Repository
steps: Confirm that the working tree is clean and that origin points to your lab304-git-workflow project.
concept: The working directory contains the files you edit. The local repository stores commits, and origin identifies the configured remote repository.

tasks.title: Make an Unstaged Change and Use git diff
steps: Append the following line to README.md:
Local change: documenting the Git workflow.
Display changes that have not been staged:
Observe the added line in the diff output, including the plus sign at the start of the added line.
Run git diff again before staging and confirm that it displays the unstaged change.
concept: git diff compares the working directory with the staging area. It shows changes that have not yet been staged; it does not show staged changes by default.

tasks.title: Stage the Change and Use git diff --cached
steps: Compare the results: after staging, the staged change should appear in git diff --cached, while git diff should be empty if no further edits were made.
concept: git diff --cached, also called git diff --staged, compares the staging area with the latest commit. It shows what would be included in the next commit.

tasks.title: Commit and Push Your Local Change
steps: Push the current branch to origin. If your branch is main and upstream tracking is already configured, use:
If upstream tracking is not configured, use git push -u origin main, substituting your actual branch name if needed.
Refresh the GitLab project page and verify that the README change and commit appear.
Check that the working tree is clean:
concept: A commit saves staged changes in the local repository. git push transfers local commits to the remote repository.

tasks.title: Create a Remote Change in GitLab
steps: Open the lab304-git-workflow project in GitLab.
Open README.md in the GitLab web editor.
Append this exact line without removing the existing content:
Remote change A: added through the GitLab web interface.
Commit the change directly to the main branch using a clear commit message, such as Add remote change A.
Do not edit README.md locally before completing the fetch and merge tasks.
concept: The remote repository now contains a commit that your local main branch has not yet incorporated. This simulates another contributor updating the shared project.

tasks.title: Use git fetch to Retrieve Remote Updates
steps: Confirm that Remote change A is not yet present in the local working file.
Compare the local branch with the fetched remote-tracking branch:
Observe that the diff shows the remote change that has not yet been integrated into local main.
concept: git fetch downloads remote commits and updates remote-tracking references such as origin/main. It does not merge those commits into the current branch or update the working files.

tasks.title: Use git merge to Integrate the Fetched Change
steps: Confirm that you are on the main branch:
Merge the fetched remote-tracking branch into your current branch:
Confirm that Remote change A is now present.

concept: git merge integrates changes from the specified branch into the current branch. In this exercise, Git may fast-forward main because the local branch has no new commits beyond the shared commit; a separate merge commit is not required.

tasks.title: Create a Second Remote Change
steps: Open README.md in the GitLab web editor again.
Append this exact line without removing existing content:
Remote change B: retrieved using git pull.
Commit the change directly to the main branch with a clear commit message, such as Add remote change B.
Do not run git fetch or git merge for this second change; the next task will demonstrate git pull.
concept: The remote main branch has advanced again. Your local branch has not yet incorporated Remote change B.

tasks.title: Use git pull to Retrieve and Integrate Remote Changes
steps: Retrieve and integrate changes from the remote main branch:
Confirm that both Remote change A and Remote change B are present.
Confirm that the working tree is clean.

concept: git pull fetches remote changes and integrates them into the current branch. Depending on the branch history and configuration, integration may be a fast-forward, a merge, or a rebase. In this lab, the local branch is behind the remote branch, so a fast-forward is normally expected.

tasks.title: Compare the Git Commands
steps: Explain the purpose of git diff.
Explain the purpose of git diff --cached.
Explain what changes after git fetch and what does not change.
Explain what git merge origin/main does after a fetch.
Explain how git pull differs from running git fetch and git merge as separate commands.
Verify that the local README contains the original content and both remote additions.

concept: git diff reviews unstaged changes; git diff --cached reviews staged changes; git fetch downloads remote updates without integrating them; git merge integrates a specified branch; git pull fetches and then integrates remote changes.

completion_message: Excellent work! You have completed Lab 304 - Git and GitLab: Diff, Fetch, Merge and Pull. You practiced reviewing unstaged and staged changes, committing and pushing local work, fetching remote updates, inspecting origin/main, merging fetched changes, and using git pull. These workflows help you understand what Git changes locally and what it retrieves from a shared repository. Keep practicing to strengthen your Linux and DevOps skills.
